summary: A 1969 list of questions about the Host-IMP protocol, such as how long a link can sit idle in a time-sharing setting and whether a host rather than its IMP should control ready-for-next-message replies. It points to the network contractor's report and asks for clarification.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 17 raises questions about how hosts and IMPs manage links and messages in the early ARPANET. The same document includes Robert Kahn's responses explaining the behavior described in the referenced protocol material.

subtitle: Questions and responses about the early Host-IMP protocol.

tldr.problem: John Kreznar questions how Host-IMP link entries, RFNMs, NOP messages and delays work in the protocol described by BBN.
tldr.mechanism: The document includes Kreznar's questions and Robert Kahn's responses explaining the link table, message queue and startup behavior.
tldr.outcome: The exchange clarifies the protocol's stated behavior; it is a discussion rather than a new protocol specification.

facts.label: Idle link-entry deletion
facts.value: After 30 seconds of disuse, if not blocked

sections.title: Questions About Links and Delays
sections.content:
John Kreznar asks whether automatic deletion of unused link entries would cause trouble for time-sharing users or for host programs delayed by other work. He asks whether hosts would need to send dummy messages just to keep links open.

Robert Kahn responds that a missing link-table entry can be inserted again when a host sends. Link entries are deleted only when they are not blocked by an active transmission; the response specifies 30 seconds of disuse for this deletion.
sections.plainLanguage: Kreznar asks whether an idle connection might disappear while a user pauses. Kahn says a host can create the link-table entry again when it sends, and active transmissions block deletion.

sections.title: RFNM and NOP Behavior
sections.content:
Kreznar asks whether the host can control RFNMs and what happens if an IMP signals readiness before the destination host accepts a message. Kahn explains that the destination IMP returns an RFNM when the message reaches the head of its output queue to the host. If it cannot deliver that message then, at most one more message may arrive; it joins the end of the queue, preserving arrival order.

Kreznar also asks why the protocol needs a discardable NOP when hosts may have to repeat transmissions. Kahn says NOP is an optional startup control message; the first message after IMP startup or after the host-ready indicator may be discarded. The response says hosts are not required to be ready to repeat transmissions into the network.
sections.plainLanguage: An RFNM is returned when a message reaches the front of the destination IMP's queue for its host. The NOP message is for startup, and the response says a host does not have to repeat network transmissions.

sections.title: A Written Clarification of the Protocol
sections.content:
The questions focus on the effects of idle links, host delays, message readiness and startup control. Kahn's response explains how the link table, output queue and startup message fit into the described Host-IMP behavior.

The document records questions and answers about an existing protocol description; it does not itself set out a replacement protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The exchange makes parts of the referenced Host-IMP description clearer by asking how they behave in specific situations. It is a clarification, not a new protocol design.
